## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(simling)
```

## The data {.smaller}

In `vot_identification`, 12 English and 12 Spanish listeners hear syllables like *ba* and *pa* made by a speech synthesiser. The [voice onset time]{.hl} (`vot`) of the first consonant goes from −20 to 60 ms in steps of 5 ms. Listeners hear each step 10 times (`trials`) and say each time whether they heard a voiced (*b*) or a voiceless (*p*) consonant; `voiceless` is how often they said *p*. Today we use only the labial consonants, *b* and *p*:

```{r}
labials <- vot_identification |>
  filter(place == "labial")
glimpse(labials)
```

Today's question: where do English and Spanish listeners put the boundary between *b* and *p*?

---

## 1. Identification curves

### 1.1 Proportions

Add a column `p`, the proportion of voiceless answers (`voiceless / trials`). Then compute the mean `p` for each `vot` and `language`, and plot it against `vot` with one colour and one line per language.

::: solution

```{r curves, eval = FALSE}
labials <- labials |>
  mutate(p = voiceless / trials)
labials |>
  summarise(p = mean(p), .by = c(vot, language)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = vot, y = p, colour = language)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  xlab("VOT (ms)") + ylab("Proportion of voiceless answers") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

:::

::: solution

```{r, ref.label = "curves", echo = FALSE}
```

Both groups go from almost always *b* to almost always *p* along an S-shaped curve. The Spanish curve rises at a shorter VOT.

:::

### 1.2 Why not `lm()`?

Why would a straight line be a poor model for these proportions?

::: solution

A straight line goes on rising below 0 and above 1, where no proportion can be. The answers flip from *b* to *p* over a narrow range of VOT, and a straight line cannot follow that S-shape.

:::

---

## 2. A logistic regression

When each row has a number of successes out of a number of trials, `glm()` takes them as `cbind(successes, failures)`: here `cbind(voiceless, trials - voiceless)`.

### 2.1 English listeners

Keep the English listeners, in a data frame `en`. Fit a logistic regression of the voiceless answers as a function of `vot` with `glm()` and `family = binomial`, and print its coefficients.

::: solution

```{r}
en <- labials |>
  filter(language == "English")
g <- glm(cbind(voiceless, trials - voiceless) ~ vot, data = en, family = binomial)
coef(g)
```

:::

### 2.2 Read the coefficients

The intercept is the log odds of a voiceless answer at a VOT of 0 ms. Turn it into a probability with `plogis()`. Then turn the slope into an odds ratio with `exp()`: what happens to the odds of a voiceless answer with each extra millisecond of VOT?

::: solution

```{r}
plogis(coef(g)[1])
exp(coef(g)[2])
```

At 0 ms, the model predicts a voiceless answer `r round(100 * plogis(coef(g)[1]), 1)`% of the time. Each extra millisecond of VOT multiplies the odds of a voiceless answer by `r round(exp(coef(g)[2]), 2)`.

:::

### 2.3 The category boundary

The boundary between *b* and *p* is the VOT at which both answers are equally likely: a probability of 0.5, or log odds of 0. Where the intercept plus the slope times `vot` is 0, `vot` is −intercept / slope. Compute the boundary. Lisker and Abramson found it at about 25 ms for English labials.

::: solution

```{r}
-coef(g)[1] / coef(g)[2]
```

The boundary lies at `r round(-coef(g)[1] / coef(g)[2], 1)` ms, close to 25 ms.

:::

---

## 3. A mixed logistic regression

### 3.1 Listeners differ

Each listener answers many times, so fit the model again with `glmer()`, with a varying intercept and a varying slope for `vot` by listener. Compare the fixed effects and the boundary with those of `g`.

::: solution

```{r}
m_en <- glmer(cbind(voiceless, trials - voiceless) ~ vot + (1 + vot | listener),
              data = en, family = binomial)
fixef(m_en)
-fixef(m_en)[1] / fixef(m_en)[2]
```

The slope is steeper than in `g`: each listener switches from *b* to *p* more abruptly than the pooled curve suggests, because listeners put their boundaries in slightly different places. The boundary is about the same.

:::

### 3.2 Two languages

Fit a mixed model to all labial data, with `vot` and `language` as predictors and the same random effects. Compute the boundary of each language. Spanish listeners should put it at a shorter VOT, about 14 ms.

::: solution

```{r}
m_lang <- glmer(cbind(voiceless, trials - voiceless) ~ vot + language + (1 + vot | listener),
                data = labials, family = binomial)
b <- fixef(m_lang)
b
c(English = -b[[1]] / b[[2]], Spanish = -(b[[1]] + b[[3]]) / b[[2]])
```

The Spanish boundary is about `r round(-b[[1]] / b[[2]] + (b[[1]] + b[[3]]) / b[[2]])` ms earlier than the English one.

:::

### 3.3 Test the difference

Fit the model without `language` and compare the two models with `anova()`. Do the languages differ?

::: solution

```{r}
m_vot <- glmer(cbind(voiceless, trials - voiceless) ~ vot + (1 + vot | listener),
               data = labials, family = binomial)
lrt <- anova(m_vot, m_lang)
lrt
```

They do: χ²(`r lrt$Df[2]`) = `r round(lrt$Chisq[2], 1)`, p `r if (lrt[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2] < 0.001) "< .001" else paste("=", round(lrt[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2], 3))`.

:::
